lessons.title: Telling Your Employer: Regime Declaration and TDS on Salary

children.text: You have done the maths and you know which regime wins. Now comes the part that actually touches your bank account: telling your employer. Get this wrong and you face a shock in February when half your salary vanishes as TDS, or a tax bill with interest when you file your return. Get it right and your monthly deductions match your real tax almost to the rupee.

body.text: For a salaried employee with no business income, the regime you declare to your employer only decides how much TDS is cut each month. Your final regime is the one you pick when you file your return.

markDefs.definition: Tax Deducted at Source. On salary, your employer estimates your tax for the whole year and deducts a share of it from each month's pay, depositing it with the government against your PAN.

children.text: Your employer is required to deduct

on salary under Section 392 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 192 of the 1961 Act). It does not deduct a flat percentage. It projects your salary for the whole tax year, applies the regime you declared along with the deductions you declared, works out the annual tax, and spreads it across the months that remain.

body.latex: \text{Monthly TDS} = \dfrac{\text{Projected annual tax} - \text{TDS already deducted}}{\text{Months remaining in the tax year}}
body.caption: Recalculated whenever your salary, declarations or proofs change. That is why TDS can jump sharply late in the year.

body.title: Estimate Monthly TDS
body.prompt: Riya joins a Kolkata consulting firm on 1 April 2026 at ₹24,00,000 a year and declares the new regime. She has no other income and no employer NPS. Assuming her salary stays constant, how much TDS will be cut each month?
body.explanation: Taxable income is ₹24,00,000 minus ₹75,000, which is ₹23,25,000. Slab tax is ₹2,00,000 up to ₹20 lakh plus 25% of ₹3,25,000 (₹81,250), total ₹2,81,250. Cess is ₹11,250, making ₹2,92,500 for the year. Divided by 12 months: ₹24,375.

body.title: The Salaried Tax Year, Month by Month

events.title: Declare your regime
events.description: Your employer asks which regime you intend to use, along with your planned investments, rent and home loan details. No declaration means the new regime is applied.

events.title: TDS based on declarations
events.description: Monthly TDS is calculated on what you declared. No proofs are needed yet.

events.title: Submit proofs
events.description: Old regime employees upload rent receipts, the landlord's PAN, 80C and 80D receipts and home loan certificates. Deadlines vary by company.

events.title: True-up
events.description: Your employer recalculates annual tax using only verified proofs and adjusts the last one or two months of TDS.

events.title: Salary TDS certificate
events.description: You receive Form 16 (or its equivalent under the new Rules), showing salary, deductions allowed and TDS deposited.

events.title: File your return
events.description: You confirm your final regime in the return, which can differ from what you told your employer if you have no business income.

children.text: What the Declaration Does and Does Not Do

columns.label: It controls
points: Which slabs and rebate your employer uses to compute TDS
Whether HRA, LTA and 80C declarations reduce your monthly TDS
The standard deduction applied in TDS: ₹75,000 or ₹50,000
What Form 16 shows at year end

columns.label: It does not control
points: Your final tax, which is settled in your return
Your final regime, if you have no business or professional income
Tax on income your employer does not know about, such as FD interest or capital gains
Whether the tax department accepts a deduction you cannot prove

body.text: Under CBDT guidance issued for the 1961 Act, an employee's regime intimation to the employer is made once for the year and cannot be changed midway. Check your employer's policy for tax year 2026-27, since some payroll systems allow a correction window. Either way, the regime you declare in April shapes TDS for the whole year.

body.title: The Default Rule
body.textWithBlank: If you do not tell your employer which regime you want, TDS on your salary is calculated under the ___ regime.
body.explanation: The new regime is the default. An employee who wants TDS calculated under the old regime must actively declare it.

children.text: The February Shock: Declaring Old, Proving Nothing

Arnav, a business analyst at a Gurugram insurer on ₹15,00,000, declared the old regime in April with ₹1,50,000 of planned 80C investments and ₹2,40,000 of HRA. His TDS for April to January was based on those numbers. Then he missed the January proof deadline: no ELSS was ever bought, and his landlord would not share a PAN.

body.caption: Arnav's TDS Before and After the Proof Deadline

children.text: After proofs rejected: ₹15,00,000 minus ₹50,000 gives ₹14,50,000. Tax is ₹1,12,500 plus 30% of ₹4,50,000 (₹1,35,000), total ₹2,47,500, plus ₹9,900 cess, which is ₹2,57,400. After ₹1,13,100 already deducted, ₹1,44,300 remains, or ₹72,150 in each of February and March.
In the new regime, his tax would have been ₹14,25,000 of taxable income: ₹60,000 plus 15% of ₹2,25,000 (₹33,750), total ₹93,750, plus ₹3,750 cess, which is ₹97,500.

body.text: Arnav's money is not lost. Since he has no business income, he can choose the new regime in his return. His true tax is ₹97,500 against ₹2,57,400 deducted, so he gets a refund of ₹1,59,900. But that refund arrives months later, while his February and March salaries were gutted. A realistic declaration in April would have avoided the whole problem.

body.title: Choosing What to Declare
body.question: Megha is unsure whether her ₹3 lakh of planned rent and 80C will actually happen this year. She values steady monthly take-home over everything else. What should she declare in April?
options: Old regime with the full ₹3 lakh, since she can always fix it later
The regime her realistic, already-committed deductions support, so TDS matches her likely final tax
Nothing at all, so her employer cannot deduct TDS
Both regimes, so her employer picks the lower TDS each month
body.explanation: Declare what you can genuinely prove. Overstating deductions lowers TDS now but causes a spike at the true-up. Not declaring simply means TDS under the new regime. There is no option to declare both.

children.text: Switching Jobs Mid-Year: The Double Rebate Trap

Tanvi worked at a Bengaluru startup from April to September on ₹1,00,000 a month, then moved to a larger company from October to March on ₹1,50,000 a month. Both employers used the new regime. Neither knew about the other salary.

body.caption: Tanvi's Two Employers vs Her Real Tax

cells: Taxable income as each saw it

body.text: Tanvi owes ₹97,500 when she files, and may also owe interest for not paying it during the year. The fix is simple: when you join a new employer, submit your previous employer's salary and TDS details (traditionally on Form 12B) so the new payroll team calculates TDS on your full-year income. Also declare the same regime to both employers unless you have a clear reason not to.

body.title: Nikhil's Declaration Dilemma
body.scenario: Nikhil, a Mumbai-based chartered accountant in an MNC's finance team, earns ₹30 lakh. His breakeven is ₹8 lakh. He pays ₹70,000 a month rent, giving roughly ₹6,40,000 of HRA exemption, and always maxes 80C and 80D. But he is negotiating to buy a flat in Thane and may stop paying rent by October.
body.prompt: Which regime should Nikhil declare to his employer in April, and what should he do if the flat purchase happens?
body.modelAnswer: With a full year of rent, his benefits are about ₹6,40,000 of HRA plus ₹1,50,000 of 80C and at least ₹25,000 of 80D, around ₹8,15,000, just above the ₹8 lakh breakeven. That makes the old regime a narrow win on paper. But if he moves in October, HRA covers only six months, roughly halving his exemption to about ₹3,20,000. His home loan interest for the remaining months will be well below ₹2 lakh, so his benefits fall far below breakeven and the new regime wins. Given the likely move, the safer declaration is the new regime. TDS will be slightly higher if he ends up not buying, but he can still choose the old regime in his return and claim a refund. Declaring old and then losing HRA would instead create a large TDS catch-up in February and March.

cards.definition: Tax your employer deducts monthly based on projected annual income and your declared regime. Section 392 of the 2025 Act (192 of the 1961 Act).
Your April statement of planned rent, 80C, 80D and home loan claims. Traditionally Form 12BB.
Documents uploaded between December and February to support old regime claims. Unproven claims are dropped.
Salary and TDS from an earlier job in the same year, given to the new employer. Traditionally Form 12B.
Annual salary TDS certificate issued by 15 June. Form numbers may change under the new Rules.
Annual Information Statement on the e-filing portal, showing salary TDS and other income reported against your PAN.

body.title: Before You Submit Your April Declaration
steps: Run the breakeven test using only deductions you are confident of for the full year
Declare the regime those realistic numbers support
If declaring old, confirm you can get rent receipts, the landlord's PAN and investment proofs
If you changed jobs this year, submit your previous employer's salary and TDS details
Tell payroll about other income or a let-out property loss if you want TDS to reflect it
Diarise your company's proof submission deadline

points: Your employer computes TDS on projected annual salary using the regime and deductions you declare.
If you declare nothing, TDS is calculated under the default new regime.
For salaried employees without business income, the employer declaration drives TDS only; the final regime is chosen in the return.
Unproven old regime deductions are dropped at the true-up, which can make February and March TDS spike sharply.
Declaring a regime your real deductions support keeps monthly TDS close to your actual tax.
When switching jobs mid-year, share your previous salary with your new employer to avoid a double rebate and a surprise bill.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax advice. Procedures and form names reflect practice under the Income-tax Act, 1961 and may change under the Income-tax Act, 2025 and its Rules. Figures are illustrative for tax year 2026-27. Consult your payroll team or a qualified tax professional.
